I believe such a message could create an unforgettable emotional connection between Samsung and its customers.

Thank you for taking the time to read my suggestion. I sincerely hope that Samsung will consider this idea and perhaps turn it into a real initiative in the future.

With my best regards,

text:
Samsung’s S26 is a perfect example of how little meaningful innovation there is in smartphones now.

Compare it with my S24: the same 50MP main camera, 10MP 3× telephoto, 12MP ultrawide, 12MP selfie camera, the same 120Hz 1080p-class display and the same 25W wired charging. Yes, the S26 has a newer processor, a slightly larger battery, newer connectivity and more AI features — but these are refinements, not a genuine generational leap.

And the AI features don't really change that for me. They’re often inconsistent, unreliable and sometimes fail to deliver what I would consider the standard of actual artificial intelligence. Adding more AI doesn't automatically make a phone more innovative. It actuly shows down productivity.

It’s becoming increasingly similar to what Apple does with the iPhone: small, incremental changes marketed as the next big generation.

The problem isn't that these phones are bad — it's the lack of ambition, imagination and genuine innovation.

When the phone in your pocket can already do 90% of what the “next generation” can do, what exactly are we upgrading for?

At what point did incremental improvements become a substitute for genuine innovation?

text:
CRITICAL UX FAILURE & EXECUTIVE ACTION REQUIRED: Restoring Fundamental Watch Behavior via Adaptive Power
Dear Samsung Electronics Executive Leadership (Product Strategy, UX Architecture, Software Engineering, and Wearable Platform Teams),
I would like to raise a critical user experience issue affecting the Galaxy Watch series.
This is not a feature request.
This is a fundamental usability issue affecting the core purpose of a watch.
Core Problem: The Removal of Raise to Wake
A watch, regardless of how advanced its technology may be, exists primarily for one essential purpose:
It must show the time immediately when the user looks at it.
For decades, the natural interaction between a person and a watch has remained unchanged. The user raises their wrist, glances at the watch, and instantly sees the time.
Galaxy Watch successfully modernized this behavior through Raise to Wake.
This feature is not merely a convenience. It is one of the foundational interactions of the entire Galaxy Watch experience.
The watch detects intentional wrist movement and immediately presents information without requiring any additional action.
This behavior is what makes a smartwatch feel like a watch.
Currently, when Power Saving Mode is enabled, Raise to Wake becomes unavailable.
This creates a contradiction.
Power Saving Mode is designed for situations where battery life becomes most valuable. Ironically, these are also the moments when users need the fastest and most efficient access to the time.
Instead of simply raising their wrist, users must touch the display or press a button.
At that moment, the device no longer behaves like a watch.
It behaves like a powered-down electronic device requiring manual activation.
Why This Creates UX Friction
Checking the time is one of the most frequent interactions performed on any watch.
Users may perform this action dozens or even hundreds of times per day.
Every additional tap, button press, or interaction introduces friction into what should be an effortless experience.
The issue becomes particularly noticeable during:
• Walking  • Driving  • Exercising  • Carrying objects  • Outdoor activities  • Professional work environments
In these situations, Raise to Wake is not a luxury feature.
It is the expected behavior of a watch.
The Contradiction of Power Saving Mode
Power Saving Mode should reduce non-essential power consumption.
However, Raise to Wake is not a non-essential function.
It is the mechanism through which the watch fulfills its primary purpose.
Reducing animations, background activity, refresh rates, sensor frequency, health monitoring intervals, and other power-intensive processes is understandable.
Removing immediate access to the time is not.
A watch that cannot conveniently show the time when the user raises their wrist undermines the fundamental reason the product is worn in the first place.
Recommended Solution: Adaptive Power Mode
Samsung could implement an Adaptive Power approach where:
• Raise to Wake remains available  • Display-on duration is shortened  • Animations are simplified  • Refresh rates are reduced  • Background activity is further optimized  • Non-critical functions remain restricted
This would preserve battery life while maintaining the fundamental identity of the product.
Strategic Business Impact
This change would:
• Improve daily usability  • Reduce user frustration  • Increase customer satisfaction  • Strengthen ecosystem loyalty  • Improve perceived software intelligence  • Reinforce Samsung's reputation for thoughtful UX design
Most importantly, it would preserve the defining interaction that makes Galaxy Watch feel like a watch.
Conclusion
Power Saving Mode should never remove the most essential interaction of a watch.
A user should always be able to raise their wrist and immediately see the time.
Raise to Wake is not a premium feature.
It is not an optional convenience.
It is one of the core foundations of the Galaxy Watch experience.
I respectfully ask Samsung's Product, UX, and Engineering teams to review this behavior and consider restoring Raise to Wake functionality within Power Saving Mode through an adaptive implementation.
Thank you for your time, consideration, and continued commitment to improving the Galaxy Watch platform.

Subject: The Omni-Lingual Architecture: Eradicating the Language Barrier for Seamless Global Understanding

To the Executive and Developer Leadership at Google Cloud, YouTube, and Samsung Electronics,

Imagine a digital reality where the concept of a "foreign language" no longer exists. A world where users watch, listen, and experience every piece of global content exactly as if it were natively created in their own mother tongue. 

Today, humanity remains isolated behind linguistic boundaries. Translation is not enough; true universality means technology becoming entirely invisible. The goal is the "Native-Tongue Illusion"—allowing anyone to seamlessly watch a video, listen to a voice, or follow a live stream from any culture, experiencing it continuously as if the entire world speaks their exact language. 

This protocol is the definitive blueprint to establish Google and Samsung as the Undisputed Infrastructure of Global Media, uniting human spirits and cultures while creating an unprecedented market moat.

CORE ARCHITECTURE: THE 3-TIERED HYBRID MODEL

1. The "Native-Tongue" Immersion (Zero-Latency AI Dubbing):
This is not merely translation; it is absolute native immersion. text:
CRITICAL UX FAILURE & EXECUTIVE ACTION REQUIRED: Restoring Fundamental Watch Behavior via Adaptive Power

Dear Samsung Electronics Executive Leadership (Product Strategy, UX Architecture, Software Engineering, and Wearable Platform Teams),

I would like to raise a critical user experience issue affecting the Galaxy Watch series.

This is not a feature request.

This is a fundamental usability issue affecting the core purpose of a watch.

Core Problem: The Removal of Raise to Wake

A watch, regardless of how advanced its technology may be, exists primarily for one essential purpose:

It must show the time immediately when the user looks at it.

For decades, the natural interaction between a person and a watch has remained unchanged. The user raises their wrist, glances at the watch, and instantly sees the time.

Galaxy Watch successfully modernized this behavior through Raise to Wake.

This feature is not merely a convenience. It is one of the foundational interactions of the entire Galaxy Watch experience.

The watch detects intentional wrist movement and immediately presents information without requiring any additional action.

This behavior is what makes a smartwatch feel like a watch.

Currently, when Power Saving Mode is enabled, Raise to Wake becomes unavailable.

This creates a contradiction.

Power Saving Mode is designed for situations where battery life becomes most valuable. Ironically, these are also the moments when users need the fastest and most efficient access to the time.

Instead of simply raising their wrist, users must touch the display or press a button.

At that moment, the device no longer behaves like a watch.

It behaves like a powered-down electronic device requiring manual activation.

Why This Creates UX Friction

Checking the time is one of the most frequent interactions performed on any watch.

Users may perform this action dozens or even hundreds of times per day.

Every additional tap, button press, or interaction introduces friction into what should be an effortless experience.

The issue becomes particularly noticeable during:

• Walking
• Driving
• Exercising
• Carrying objects
• Outdoor activities
• Professional work environments

In these situations, Raise to Wake is not a luxury feature.

It is the expected behavior of a watch.

The Contradiction of Power Saving Mode

Power Saving Mode should reduce non-essential power consumption.

However, Raise to Wake is not a non-essential function.

It is the mechanism through which the watch fulfills its primary purpose.

Reducing animations, background activity, refresh rates, sensor frequency, health monitoring intervals, and other power-intensive processes is understandable.

Removing immediate access to the time is not.

A watch that cannot conveniently show the time when the user raises their wrist undermines the fundamental reason the product is worn in the first place.

Recommended Solution: Adaptive Power Mode

Samsung could implement an Adaptive Power approach where:

• Raise to Wake remains available
• Display-on duration is shortened
• Animations are simplified
• Refresh rates are reduced
• Background activity is further optimized
• Non-critical functions remain restricted

This would preserve battery life while maintaining the fundamental identity of the product.

Strategic Business Impact

This change would:

• Improve daily usability
• Reduce user frustration
• Increase customer satisfaction
• Strengthen ecosystem loyalty
• Improve perceived software intelligence
• Reinforce Samsung's reputation for thoughtful UX design

Most importantly, it would preserve the defining interaction that makes Galaxy Watch feel like a watch.

Conclusion

Power Saving Mode should never remove the most essential interaction of a watch.

A user should always be able to raise their wrist and immediately see the time.

Raise to Wake is not a premium feature.

It is not an optional convenience.

It is one of the core foundations of the Galaxy Watch experience.

I respectfully ask Samsung's Product, UX, and Engineering teams to review this behavior and consider restoring Raise to Wake functionality within Power Saving Mode through an adaptive implementation.

Thank you for your time, consideration, and continued commitment to improving the Galaxy Watch platform

text:
@samsung Combining a wide f/1.4 aperture with a large sensor like the 1/1.12" or 1/1.28" is essentially the "Holy Grail" of mobile photography. When you pair a massive physical opening with a massive surface area for catching light, you move away from "phone quality" and start approaching the physics of dedicated mirrorless cameras.
​Here is what happens when those two specific technologies collide:
​1. Extreme Light Gathering (The "Night Owl" Effect)
​The most immediate benefit is low-light performance.
​Sensor Size: A 1/1.12" sensor has much larger individual pixels (or "super-pixels" when binning) than a standard sensor.
​Aperture: The f/1.4 opening allows a massive volume of photons to hit those pixels.
Together, this combo can capture bright, clean images in environments where the human eye struggles to see, reducing the need for aggressive "Night Mode" long exposures that often cause motion blur.
​2. Natural Optical Bokeh
​Most phones use software (AI) to blur the background in Portrait Mode. However, a large sensor combined with an f/1.4 aperture creates natural depth of field.
​The transition between the sharp subject and the blurred background (the "fall-off") is much smoother and more professional.
​You won't see those "cut-out" errors around hair or glasses that software often misses.
​3. The "Thin Focus" Challenge
​While bigger is usually better, this combination introduces a specific technical hurdle: a very shallow plane of focus.
​With a sensor as big as 1/1.12" and an aperture at f/1.4, the "slice" of the image that is in focus is extremely thin.
​If you take a close-up photo of a person, their eyes might be sharp, but their nose and ears could be blurred. This is why many manufacturers (like Huawei or Xiaomi) now use Variable Aperture—allowing the camera to stop down to f/4.0 when you need the whole scene to be sharp.
